processing: Green or black base tea takes on aroma from vanilla, using an adsorption method: the tea absorbs the scent of the spice rather than being sprayed with a flavouring, by the makers' account.
harvest_season: No picking season is documented for this tea; it is a scented product made from finished base tea, so the season of the base matters more than any date on the scenting.
appearance_dry: Little is recorded; expect the look of its base, a green or black loose leaf, with a noticeable vanilla smell.
appearance_liquor: The green version is a bright yellow-green; the black version is a bright, vivid red.
appearance_wet: Little is recorded; as with other scented teas, the wet leaf looks like its base tea.
taste_profile: The green version smells fresh and clean with a mellow body and a sweet return. The black version is sweet-scented, strong and brisk, and works with milk or cold.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for the green version, Western-style. For the black version use water just off the boil; try it with milk or chilled.

vintage_note: Sold as a ready scented product, not by vintage or named harvest. As is usual for scented teas, the aroma is the first thing to fade, so buy recent stock, keep it sealed and drink it within about a year.
description:
Xianglan Cha is Hainan's vanilla tea: green or black tea scented with vanilla pods. It is a modern product, not an old regional tea, and it is often listed among the island's speciality teas next to far older names.

The idea is the same as jasmine tea with a different plant. Dry tea readily takes up smells, and the makers use that to carry vanilla into the leaf. Accounts describe premium base tea and a modern adsorption method, without much further detail.

The two versions behave differently. The green is the gentler one, yellow-green in the cup with a mellow, sweet finish. The black is bright red, strong and brisk, and it is said to be at its best with milk or served cold. Do not expect much development across steeps; as with most scented teas, the first two carry the aroma.

When buying, ask which base you are getting and smell the leaf. Plenty of vanilla teas on the market rely on added flavouring, and the name on the packet alone will not tell you how this one was scented.
history:
Accounts agree that the tea did not exist in Hainan before 1993, when Hainan Xiangsheng Natural Food Co. developed it together with the food science college of Southwest Agricultural University. That is the company story as repeated in Chinese tea listings; little independent documentation is available.

Its health claims, repeated in promotional writing, have no solid support and are best ignored.
